opus-5.5.text:
I think a useful way to frame it is that both prompting and fine-tuning are ways of steering the model toward a particular part of the distribution it has already learned. A pretrained language model has seen an enormous amount of text, so in some sense it already "knows" how to do a lot of different things. The question is how you get it to actually express the behavior you want, rather than some other plausible continuation.

Prompting does that by changing the input. You're giving the model context so that, conditioned on what you've written, the continuation you want becomes the most likely one. It's cheap and flexible, and you don't touch the weights at all, which is nice. You can iterate quickly. But it's also somewhat brittle. Small changes in wording or in the ordering of examples can lead to surprisingly large changes in performance, and you're limited by the context window and by how well the model can infer what you mean from a handful of examples or instructions.

Fine-tuning changes the model itself. You're updating the parameters on data that reflects the behavior you want, so you're more directly reshaping the distribution. That tends to be more reliable for a specific task, and it can teach things that are hard to get across in a prompt. The downsides are that it costs more compute, you need data, and you can lose some generality. The model may become very good at one thing and forget or degrade on others.

I don't see them as completely separate, though. They sit on a spectrum of how much you intervene on the model. Things like prompt tuning or prefix tuning fall right in between: you learn the input rather than writing it by hand. And a lot of my interest is in how far you can push the prompting end. If the model already has the capability latent in it, can we design prompts that teach it a procedure, almost like an algorithm, so it executes it reliably without any weight updates? That's where I think prompting gets really interesting, because it starts to look less like asking nicely and more like a form of in-context programming.

r001.rationale: It says prompting changes the input so the desired continuation becomes most likely, explaining how prompt information constrains plausible outputs.

r002.rationale: It says fine-tuning updates parameters on data reflecting the desired behavior and reshapes the distribution, making that behavior more reliable for the task.

r003.rationale: It frames both methods as steering the model to express the desired behavior instead of another plausible continuation.

fable-5.1.text:
The way I think about it is that a pretrained language model is kind of this huge, messy distribution over possible behaviors. It's seen the whole internet, so it has latent in it the ability to act like a helpful expert, or a confused forum poster, or a textbook, or someone trolling. And when you want a particular output, your real job is to steer the model into the region of that distribution where the behavior you want lives.

Prompting and fine-tuning are both ways of doing that steering, they just operate on different levers. With prompting, you're conditioning. You're not changing the model at all, you're giving it context that makes the behavior you want much more likely under the distribution it already has. That's why things like chain-of-thought work: you're not teaching the model to reason, you're putting it in a context where the kind of text that follows tends to look like careful step-by-step reasoning, and the model has seen a lot of that. The same with role prompts or few-shot examples. You're saying, "here's what the neighborhood looks like, stay in it."

Fine-tuning is actually moving the weights, so you're reshaping the distribution itself rather than navigating it. The thing I find interesting is that for a lot of behaviors, fine-tuning is doing something that looks surprisingly similar to prompting, just baked in. Instruction tuning, for example, is in some sense teaching the model to behave as if there's always a certain kind of prompt in front of it, even when there isn't. You're amortizing the conditioning into the parameters. And that's part of why it's data-efficient in a way that's surprising if you think of it as "learning a new skill." You're often not teaching new capabilities, you're making existing ones the default.

Where they genuinely differ is in what happens when the behavior you want isn't already well represented. If the pretrained model just doesn't have a good concept of some domain or some format, you can prompt all day and you'll get something that pattern-matches on the surface but falls apart. There, fine-tuning can actually add something. But it's also more dangerous, because you can degrade the general capabilities you were relying on, and you don't always notice until you probe it.

So my working heuristic is: prompting tells you what the model can already do, and fine-tuning tells you what it can be made to do reliably. I usually want to exhaust prompting first, not just because it's cheap, but because it's diagnostic. If I can't get the behavior at all with a good prompt, that tells me something about whether the capability is really there, and that shapes what kind of fine-tuning I should even attempt.

r001.rationale: It says prompting conditions the model with context that makes the desired behavior more likely within its existing distribution, which explains how prompt information narrows plausible outputs.

r002.rationale: It says fine-tuning moves the weights and reshapes the distribution so desired behaviors can become the model’s default or more reliable.

r003.rationale: The response says both methods steer toward desired behavior, but does not clearly state that their shared aim is to make the user’s desired output the model’s most likely output.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as two ways of steering a model toward the behavior you want. With prompting, you keep the model fixed and put the specification in its context: an instruction, a few examples, or some information it needs to answer the question. With fine-tuning, you provide training examples and update the model’s parameters, so that the desired behavior becomes something it has learned rather than something you have to describe each time.

What’s interesting is that the distinction isn’t simply that prompting gives you information and fine-tuning gives you skills. Examples in a prompt can also help a model infer what task you’re asking it to do, or what kind of answer you expect. And fine-tuning can change things like style and format without necessarily teaching a fundamentally new capability.

So I’d usually start with prompting, because it’s easy to experiment with and revise. If you have a well-defined task, enough good examples, and you want consistent behavior across many inputs, fine-tuning becomes attractive. And they’re complementary—you still prompt a fine-tuned model. The practical question is which parts of the behavior you want to learn from data and which parts you want to specify at the moment you use it.

r001.rationale: It says prompting puts a specification in the model’s context and steers behavior, but does not explain that this constrains the space of plausible outputs.

r002.rationale: It describes fine-tuning as updating parameters so desired behavior is learned, but does not explain that this increases the likelihood assigned to desired outputs.

r003.rationale: It describes a shared aim of steering toward desired behavior, but does not identify the aim as making the model’s most likely output match the user’s desired output.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of prompting and fine-tuning as two ways of steering a model toward the behavior you want. With prompting, you keep the model’s parameters fixed and put information in the context: an instruction, a few examples, or some combination of those. With fine-tuning, you use examples to update the parameters themselves.

What’s interesting is that the distinction can be less clear in practice than it sounds. Giving examples in a prompt can look a lot like learning a task, even though no weights are changing. And fine-tuning can teach a model how to respond to prompts, so the two methods work together.

The practical question is where you want that information to live. Prompting makes it easy to change your instructions or examples from one request to the next. Fine-tuning lets you make a behavior more persistent, but it requires training data and an additional optimization step. In either case, you still have to check whether the model has learned what you intended, rather than just producing outputs that look right on the examples you tried.

r001.rationale: The response says prompting adds instructions or examples to context and steers behavior, but does not explain that this constrains the space of plausible outputs.

r002.rationale: It describes fine-tuning as updating parameters with examples, but does not say this increases the likelihood of desired types of outputs.

r003.rationale: It gives a shared aim of steering toward wanted behavior, but does not state that both methods aim to make the user's desired output the model's most likely output.
